In a clinical trial involving 120 healthy people, participants were given omeprazole. None had heartburn or acid reflux at the start of the trial, yet afterward, nearly half developed heartburn, indigestion, or acid reflux.

Acid reflux isn’t always a problem of too much stomach acid. In fact, many people with GERD and acid reflux may actually have low stomach acid.

Antacids aren’t meant to be taken long term; however, many people use them for extended periods. Side effects associated with long-term use can include nutritional deficiencies, anxiety, depression, and more.

Overeating, a hiatal hernia, and high-sugar diets can also contribute to heartburn and acid reflux.

Betaine hydrochloride can help acidify the stomach and may help reduce GERD symptoms. Zinc carnosine can also support digestive health if you’re dealing with an ulcer or stomach inflammation.

videos.summary_source_text:
Optimize Your Drives #golfswing #golftips If you’re hitting down on your driver or fighting a steep downswing, this simple setup drill will change everything. 
Place an alignment stick behind the ball and a head cover just in front — then focus on swinging under the stick and over the head cover. 
You’ll shallow the club naturally, improve your path, and start hitting up on the ball for better launch and distance.

Stop Doing C-Cuts Skate Like This Instead The Downhill Skating System is the mechanics-first approach that unlocks effortless, controlled speed on the ice without extra conditioning, pushing or “trying harder.” Inspired by the movement signatures of players like Connor McDavid, Nathan MacKinnon, Cale Makar, Quinn Hughes, and other elite NHL skaters, this system teaches you how to move on the ice with gravity, using your body's own stretch shortening cycles mixed with the most efficient footwork patterns and various skating mechanics.

Most players skate “uphill”: stiff, blocky, pushing hard, creating tension and burning energy like we were always taught in traditional powerskating. Downhill skating flips that model. By using counter rotation, proper joint angles, and natural gravitational momentum, we teach you move faster with less effort.

Inside the Downhill Skating System, players learn to:

1) Unlock the inner spring for better acceleration.
2)Use different footwork patterns to add options, deception and effortlessness. 
3)Proper joint alignment for efficiency and balance instead of creating tension with push strides.

Apply NHL-base mechanics like shin angle, Y-angle, rhythm and cadence. Generate speed using the rocker, with heel pressure and subtle weight transfers.

This system is not what players would learn in traditional, outdated power skating methods. It’s a biomechanics-based operating system designed to match your body type and natural movement patterns.

Whether you’re trying to improve the forward stride, lateral movements, deception, or posture, Downhill Skating reveals the hidden mechanics the NHL’s best rely on, and shows you how to plug them into your game step by step.

If you’re ready to skate faster with less effort, flow through transitions, and move with the smoothness of the world’s best players, the Downhill Skating System is your blueprint to faster player development.

videos.title: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Is a Freak: 552B Parameters, Only 8B Active
videos.summary_source_text:
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Is a Freak: 552B Parameters, Only 8B Active https://bitbiased.ai/ai-automation-services

DeepSeek says V4.1-Flash scored 90.6 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, ahead of Claude Opus 5 at 89.1 and GPT-5.6 Sol at 88.8. Even more striking: this is a 552-billion-parameter model that activates just 8 billion parameters per input token.

But that headline needs context.

DeepSeek V4.1-Flash arrived on September 10 with open weights under an MIT license, native vision, a one-million-token context window, and an architecture designed around a simple reality of AI agents: they spend far more tokens reading than writing. DeepSeek's answer is to make that reading dramatically cheaper.

One real-world test shows why this matters. DataCamp gave V4.1-Flash a screenshot of a broken Flask dashboard and access to the underlying project. Without being told where the bugs were, the agent identified problems across Python, CSS, and JavaScript and produced a three-file patch. All five tests passed.

Then there was a problem: the webpage was still wrong.

The agent correctly diagnosed that the Flask server was running stale code, but it had no tool to restart it before hitting its turn limit. A human restart was required. It's a useful example of the difference between fixing code and actually completing an autonomous software task.

The entire run involved 156,724 input tokens, with an 87% cache hit rate, plus 11,497 output tokens. Reported off-peak cost: about one cent.

That efficiency comes from some unusual architecture. V4.1-Flash combines mixture-of-experts routing with a split encoder-decoder design. DeepSeek says only 8 billion parameters are active per token during input processing and 16 billion during generation. Its KV cache is also just 890 bytes per token, using compressed sparse attention, 4-bit cache storage, and on-demand reconstruction.

At DeepSeek's off-peak pricing, cached input costs $0.003 per million tokens. That sounds almost absurdly cheap—but price per token isn't necessarily price per completed task.

So we go through DeepSeek's benchmark table line by line.

V4.1-Flash scores 90.6 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, 74.2 on DeepSWE, 88.1 on CyberGym, and 54.8 on AutomationBench. But harder benchmarks tell a different story. On Terminal-Bench 3.0 it scores 30.0 versus 43.3 for Claude Opus 5, while Terminal-Bench 4.0 shows 31.2 versus 51.8. DeepSeek's own results also show that changing the agent harness can move its DeepSWE score from 65.5 to 74.2.

Then there's the competition DeepSeek's original chart didn't include. Around the same period, newer models arrived from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and xAI, including GPT-6 Luna, GPT-6 Sol, Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 3.8 Flash, and Grok 4.7. That changes how V4.1-Flash's headline comparisons should be interpreted.

Independent Artificial Analysis testing adds another piece: V4.1-Flash scored 39 on its Intelligence Index versus 36 for V4-Pro and reached roughly 227 tokens per second. But it also generated substantially more output tokens than the median comparable model, pushing its measured cost per task to $0.27.

So is DeepSeek V4.1-Flash actually a frontier-model killer, or is its real achievement something more interesting: making long-context, input-heavy AI agents dramatically cheaper to run?

We break down the architecture, pricing, benchmarks, independent testing, limitations, and what DeepSeek's upcoming V4.1-Pro could mean next. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}

But that headline needs context.

DeepSeek V4.1-Flash arrived on September 10 with open weights under an MIT license, native vision, a one-million-token context window, and an architecture designed around a simple reality of AI agents: they spend far more tokens reading than writing. DeepSeek's answer is to make that reading dramatically cheaper.

One real-world test shows why this matters. DataCamp gave V4.1-Flash a screenshot of a broken Flask dashboard and access to the underlying project. Without being told where the bugs were, the agent identified problems across Python, CSS, and JavaScript and produced a three-file patch. All five tests passed.

Then there was a problem: the webpage was still wrong.

The agent correctly diagnosed that the Flask server was running stale code, but it had no tool to restart it before hitting its turn limit. A human restart was required. It's a useful example of the difference between fixing code and actually completing an autonomous software task.

The entire run involved 156,724 input tokens, with an 87% cache hit rate, plus 11,497 output tokens. Reported off-peak cost: about one cent.

That efficiency comes from some unusual architecture. V4.1-Flash combines mixture-of-experts routing with a split encoder-decoder design. DeepSeek says only 8 billion parameters are active per token during input processing and 16 billion during generation. Its KV cache is also just 890 bytes per token, using compressed sparse attention, 4-bit cache storage, and on-demand reconstruction.

At DeepSeek's off-peak pricing, cached input costs $0.003 per million tokens. That sounds almost absurdly cheap—but price per token isn't necessarily price per completed task.

So we go through DeepSeek's benchmark table line by line.

V4.1-Flash scores 90.6 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, 74.2 on DeepSWE, 88.1 on CyberGym, and 54.8 on AutomationBench. But harder benchmarks tell a different story. On Terminal-Bench 3.0 it scores 30.0 versus 43.3 for Claude Opus 5, while Terminal-Bench 4.0 shows 31.2 versus 51.8. DeepSeek's own results also show that changing the agent harness can move its DeepSWE score from 65.5 to 74.2.

Then there's the competition DeepSeek's original chart didn't include. Around the same period, newer models arrived from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and xAI, including GPT-6 Luna, GPT-6 Sol, Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 3.8 Flash, and Grok 4.7. That changes how V4.1-Flash's headline comparisons should be interpreted.

Independent Artificial Analysis testing adds another piece: V4.1-Flash scored 39 on its Intelligence Index versus 36 for V4-Pro and reached roughly 227 tokens per second. But it also generated substantially more output tokens than the median comparable model, pushing its measured cost per task to $0.27.

So is DeepSeek V4.1-Flash actually a frontier-model killer, or is its real achievement something more interesting: making long-context, input-heavy AI agents dramatically cheaper to run?

videos.title: “Fable 5.2” Just DESTROYED GPT-6 Astra
videos.summary_source_text:
“Fable 5.2” Just DESTROYED GPT-6 Astra https://bitbiased.ai/ai-automation-services

A supposed “Fable 5.2” is being credited with beating GPT-6 Astra, quietly appearing inside Claude Code, and delivering major coding and visual-generation upgrades. But there’s one problem: Anthropic has never announced a model called Fable 5.2.

As of September 21st, Anthropic’s official page still lists Claude Fable 5.1 as its most capable model for ambitious coding projects. There’s no Fable 5.2 model ID, pricing page, system card, benchmark table, or launch announcement.

So where did the rumor come from — and is there actually a secret Anthropic model being tested?

The trail starts on September 1st, when investor Gavin Baker speculated that Anthropic might already have “Fable 5.2” ready. After OpenAI released GPT-6 Astra on September 3rd, that speculation accelerated. Within days, social-media posts were claiming Anthropic’s next Fable could come from an entirely new pretraining run and arrive by late September or early October.

Then users began claiming they were actually encountering the mystery model inside Claude Code.

Some testers reported that Fable 5.1 sessions appeared to be routing to a “next Fable” model. One unusual test involved asking Claude about “Tibo the reset guy,” with users treating knowledge of that recent niche reference as evidence that they had reached a newer checkpoint.

But that test has a major problem: getting the answer right doesn’t reveal which model produced it. Different post-training data, hidden context, memory, retrieval, A/B testing, effort settings, or another checkpoint could potentially produce the same result.

Anthropic does officially document model routing in certain circumstances, so the underlying infrastructure exists. What hasn’t surfaced is an API model identifier, network artifact, billing identifier, leaked system card, or other technical evidence proving regular users are secretly being routed to “Fable 5.2.”

The viral demos have similar limitations. One Reddit user reported that a suspected newer model made real progress on coding projects where Fable 5.1 had struggled, including choosing a state-machine architecture for a Rust networking protocol. A September 19th visual comparison also appeared to show the mystery model going head-to-head with GPT-6 Astra.

Interesting evidence — but neither confirms the backend model.

There’s another complication: Fable 5.1 is already extremely capable. videos.summary_source_text: This Mobility Test Explains Your Swing  #golfswing #golftips This simple 90/90 mobility test gives you a clear look at how your right arm should function in the golf swing. From a 5-iron posture, lift and rotate the arm until it matches your spine angle—if you can’t get there, your backswing is likely compensating by standing up or losing posture. That compensation often leads to poor ball striking and inconsistent contact. Your swing should reflect what your body can actually do, even if that means a shorter backswing. videos.summary_source_text:
Before Hitting Your Woods - Make This 5 Second Change Fairway woods and hybrids should make golf easier… but for a lot of golfers they’re some of the hardest clubs in the bag to hit consistently.

Tops, thin shots, heavy strikes and weak shots to the right can quickly destroy your confidence.

And according to Shot Scope, the average golfer uses a fairway wood or hybrid for around 25% of their shots — so learning how to strike them properly can make a huge difference to your scores.

In this golf lesson, Danny Maude shows you two simple drills to help you hit your fairway woods and hybrids cleaner, straighter and with more distance.

The first drill helps you improve your ball striking and understand how the club should travel through impact.

The second helps you create more speed and naturally square the clubface — without trying to manipulate your golf swing.

If you struggle to hit fairway woods off the ground, top your 3 wood, thin your hybrids or slice them to the right, this lesson should really help.

You’ll discover:

• Why golfers top fairway woods and hybrids  
• Why thin shots can happen for a completely different reason  
• The ideal strike for a fairway wood off the ground  
• A simple finish position that can improve your contact  
• Why the trail shoulder matters through impact  
• How to create a shallow, sweeping strike with fairway woods  
• The ball position I recommend for a fairway wood  
• A simple drill you can use before you play  
• Why forcing positions can make your swing feel wooden  
• How opening the clubface can actually help a golfer who slices  
• How to square the clubface naturally through impact  
• Why releasing the club can create more speed and distance  
• How to hit fairway woods with a powerful sweeping motion  
• How to know whether you are too steep or leaning back in your golf swing  

One of the biggest mistakes golfers make with fairway woods is trying to lift the golf ball into the air.

The club already has loft.

Your job is to create a strike where the club travels beautifully through the ball and brushes the turf — allowing the loft of the club to launch the golf ball for you.

Once you understand that sensation, fairway woods and hybrids can start to feel dramatically easier.
